title: Negotiating $25 an hour in Louis B. Mayer's office
summary: In a meeting in Mayer's office Lee got his $500 and demanded $25 an hour, not scale, for teaching Mickey Rooney.

story.theme_name: Jazz musicians in the movies and film scoring
story.community_name: Studio work and jingles: New York session life

blocks.x: Now, at the time, the scale for rehearsal time was $15 an hour for a musician, you know -- no, I'm sorry, it was $5 -- it's $15 now. It was $5 an hour. Okay, so I was always kind of a good businessman, you know, where my performance was, you know; I would ask for good money.

So I felt as though they owed me something because of the way they bruised me. And so we got in there, and George Georgia said, "Well what happened?" And I told him what happened, I was promised $500 -- and if it had taken me 3 weeks to do it, I wouldn't have expected any more than $500, you know, but since it just took 6 hours, you know, I thought I was entitled to my money. And so they said, well, okay, "You're gonna get your $500. You'll get the balance. Are you satisfied?" I said, "Well, now let's find out what I'm gonna get for teaching him." And they said, "Well, the scale is $5 an hour." It was either $5 or $7.50 an hour; I don't remember what it was.
I said, "I don't work for scale." You know. No one had told me that, you know; I just knew -- I just knew that I had them, you know. I said, "I don't work for scale."

He said, "Well, what do you want?" I said, "I want $25 an hour." "You want $25 an hour?" I said, "I want $25 an hour for teaching him, and every day that I come to the set, whether if you call me and it's an 8 hour day, or what."

And -- I made the deal. And I got it. And I was there so many days -- you know, when they're shooting, they had to have me there because they didn't know when they would get to me -- when they would get to the part where they needed me.
But I taught him every lick of it, and I recorded "Strike Up the Band." I don't know if you ever saw the picture, but ...
